content.text: Application validation and database constraints do different jobs. Validation tells a user what's wrong with their input; a constraint is the only rule that holds for every writer and every pair of concurrent requests. In a test on SQL Server 2022, two sessions both checked that an email was free, both saw 0 rows and both inserted it. With a
constraint, the second insert failed with error 2627.

The signup endpoint checks whether an email is taken before it inserts the user, and the validator has unit tests. Still, the users table has two accounts for the same address, created by a double tap on "Create account". In a test on SQL Server 2022, two sessions reproduced it: each checked the email and saw 0 rows, then each inserted, and the table held two rows for
. Wrapping each session's check and insert in a transaction at the default isolation level didn't help: the same interleaving committed two rows again.
The belief: if the application validates data before saving it,

The reasoning sounds solid. The validation layer is where the rules live in code, covered by tests and returning clear messages per field. A database error arrives late, as an ugly exception. Constraints look like the same rule written twice, in migrations nobody likes to touch, and some teams treat the database as plain storage behind an ORM. Validation is genuinely needed. It just can't do a constraint's job.
A check and a write are two separate moments
The application's check reads the table at one moment, and the insert writes at another. Two requests for the same email can both read before either one writes: a classic
. A transaction doesn't close that gap at
, SQL Server's default: Microsoft's table lists phantoms as allowed at that level, and a row that appears after you looked for it is exactly that. A

constraint closes the gap because the database checks uniqueness as part of the insert itself, against a unique index it creates for the constraint. In the test, with the constraint in place, the second session's insert failed with error 2627 and the table kept one row.
Your application isn't the only writer

Data arrives through admin scripts, bulk imports, a second service, a background job, a support tool, a migration that backfills a column, or a new endpoint whose author forgot the validator. Validation protects the code path it lives in. A constraint applies to every statement, whoever sends it: PostgreSQL's docs say an error is raised whenever someone tries to store data that violates a constraint, even when the value came from a column default. Constraints also outlive the code. Applications get rewritten; the data stays.
